absent: Mount reference acquisition, fast release, expiry insertion, and namespace attach or detach paths outside the slow release fragment.
Full dentry kill, unlink, inode eviction, and least-recently-used shrinker trigger behavior beyond list draining.
Delayed mount release worker, per-task work completion, and RCU free callbacks for mounts and superblocks.
Superblock allocation, lookup, shared-batch inode numbering state, shrinker registration, and filesystem specific kill and statistics implementations.
Security option, credential, user namespace, network namespace, and module lifetime semantics beyond acquire and release calls.
Filesystem notification delivery effects for mount deletion and waiter wakeup protocol for superblock flags.
Monolithic mount data parsing, source string handling, and final mount materialization from a filesystem context.
Asynchronous I/O file, request and context usage of anonymous inodes and pseudo superblock operations.
Multigrain timestamp query marking, counter storage, tracing hooks, and clock source accuracy guarantees.

findings.text: Public dentry reference and reclaim helpers allow taking an extra reference, attempting a fast release, otherwise queueing a zero-count dentry onto a caller supplied shrink list, and later draining such a list from the tail with per-dentry locking and chained killing until empty.

Mount usage query helpers expose total reference count and total write holder count, aggregating per processor counters where multiprocessing is present and using a single scalar otherwise, plus filesystem module reference acquire and release around mount lifetime.

Superblock release helpers expose a two level interface where an outer release drops activity unless last, and inner locked handling destroys shrinker and list structures, invokes filesystem teardown and notification, then drops passive reference with RCU deferred destruction and list unlinking under a global lock.

Kernel internal mount construction exposes long term mount creation from a filesystem type, generic kernel mount with flags plus name and opaque data, context allocation for mount purposes, and monolithic option dispatch with a generic fallback when the filesystem provides no parser.

Anonymous and asynchronous I/O inode provisioning exposes creation of pseudo inodes with fresh numbers and private untyped ownership, cache backed allocation and release for the async subsystem, pseudo context initialization with magic plus no-user and no-execution device restrictions, and early subsystem bootstrap that aborts on mount failure.

Inode time and initialization helpers expose setting access modification and change times from a supplied value, truncating stamps to superblock range and granularity, refreshing change time with coarse or fine clock selection, initializing all three stamps together, and zeroing plus list and mapping initialization for new inodes and address spaces.

A mount transitions to teardown at most once by requiring detached namespace context, a zero aggregated count after decrement, absence of a prior doomed mark, then setting doomed while still excluding concurrent releasers before detaching instance linkage and expiry linkage and asserting no attached children remain.

Multiprocessor mount accounting observes all release counters before all acquisition counters with an ordering barrier between the passes, so a release counted in the first pass necessarily has its matching acquisition visible in the second pass, while uniprocessor builds use direct scalar counts.

Shrink list membership pairs flag changes with unused accounting such that addition sets both shrink and least-recently-used markers with an increment, removal clears both with a decrement, only zero-count entries without existing shrink membership are queued, and least-recently-used membership is removed first when present.

A mountpoint object is freed only when both its mount list and cover list are empty, at which point the mounted marker is cleared under dentry lock, the dentry reference is transferred to a shrink list, and hash linkage plus object storage are released; cover removal also uses RCU deferred storage release.

Superblock death is announced exactly once under a global spin lock by setting a single dead flag with release ordering followed by a barrier and variable wakeup, after dropping any device table claim, so later lookups skip the object and concurrent waiters either discard it or wait for completion.

Anonymous inode numbers are never zero and multiprocessor allocation reserves numbers in batches through a shared atomic counter with per processor caching, while anonymous inodes start dirty and private with user read-write mode, current ownership, a no-op dirty mapping operation set, and identical initial access modification and change stamps.

Mount context creation records purpose, flags, filesystem reference, credentials, network namespace and logging prefix, then purpose selects user namespace source and whether to pin activity and hold a root dentry; teardown reverses root, filesystem specific state, security options, namespaces, credentials, log, type reference and storage, with log storage freed only when its last user drops.

Change time updates for multigrain inodes compare coarse time against queried state, escalate to fine clock only when needed, skip atomic update when seconds and subseconds already match, otherwise attempt an atomic subsecond swap followed by ordered seconds publication with one retry when the only change was concurrent marking as queried, else preserve the observed existing stamp; non-multigrain inodes take a direct set path.

Timestamp truncation clamps seconds into the superblock minimum and maximum, zeroes subseconds at either clamp boundary, leaves nanosecond granularity unchanged, zeroes subseconds for one second granularity, quantizes down to a multiple of intermediate granularity, and warns on out of range granularity values.

Mount hash and instance mutations are serialized by the write side of a sequence lock held across count decrement and validation, doomed marking, instance unlinking, expiry detachment and cover traversal, with read-side critical section exit ordered inside the locked region before final unlock and shrink processing.

Dentry shrink transitions and mounted-marker changes require the per-dentry spin lock, covering queueing onto a shrink list, removal from shrink accounting, transfer of mountpoint dentries to a shrink list, and the lock release paired with shrink queueing in the dput-to-list path.

Superblock teardown uses an exclusive read-write semaphore for last-activity handling with shared mode available for non-exclusive users, a global spin lock for super list and instance unlinking and dead-flag publication, and ordered release that unlocks exclusively when activity remains but proceeds to destruction when activity reaches zero.

Filesystem pin teardown combines read-side RCU protection over pin list observation with an interrupt-safe per-pin wait lock around completion state changes and waiter queueing, while address space and inode setup initializes mapping semaphore and private lock, per-inode migration lock for async inodes, and an optional size sequence counter depending on configuration.

The mount object as observed carries namespace membership, nested mount flags and root plus superblock pointers, per-superblock forward and back linkage, identifier and per-processor accounting storage, expiry and child lists, cover hash, pin list, write holder accounting, deferred release list and callback state, and an internal marker distinguishing synchronous from deferred destruction.

The dentry shrink view as observed carries a least-recently-used linkage reused for shrink lists, a spin lock plus combined lock and reference counter, flag bits for shrink membership recency mounted state and killed state, while mountpoint and cover objects carry hash linkage, mount and cover lists, back pointer to dentry, and RCU callback state.

The superblock view as observed carries active and passive reference counts, a read-write unmount semaphore, shrinker and filesystem type pointers, flag word, dentry and inode least-recently-used structures, global list and instance hash linkage, mount list head, user namespace, device table handle, time range and granularity, and RCU callback state; device handles carry reference count, table node, back pointer and RCU state.

The mount context view as observed carries purpose, superblock flags and mask, filesystem type reference, credentials, network and user namespaces, optional pinned root dentry, operations vector, private filesystem data, global marker, security options, source string, logging prefix plus shared log with per-slot ownership bitmap, and a flag controlling filesystem specific release.

The inode and mapping view as observed carries number, mode, ownership, state and operation flags, superblock pointer, mapping with page tree plus semaphore private lock and cached tree root, device input-output writeback least-recently-used and superblock lists, hash node, size sequencing state, and split seconds plus subseconds for access modification and change times; async inodes wrap a base inode with a context pointer and migration lock.

The async filesystem binding as observed pairs allocation and release operations with a simple statistics operation in a super operations table, selects that table during filesystem context initialization after pseudo context setup, and the early bootstrap registers a filesystem descriptor carrying a name plus context setup and anonymous teardown operations.

Mount slow release moves from counted to zero-validated to doomed to detached to destroyed, with internal mounts destroyed synchronously in the releaser and other mounts first attempting per-task deferred work for non-kernel threads, otherwise queueing on a delayed list with a scheduled worker, and returning early whenever count remains nonzero or doomed was already set.

Dentry shrink draining repeatedly removes the tail entry from accounting under lock, frees it immediately when already marked killed, otherwise invokes chained killing that follows victim succession until no victim remains, continuing until the supplied list is empty.

Superblock release moves from active counting to exclusive locking on last activity to atomic last-check, then either unlocks when activity reappeared or proceeds through shrinker release, filesystem teardown, death notification, least-recently-used destruction and passive release to RCU deferred final destruction with type reference dropped last.

Mount final cleanup orders writer validation, pin killing, filesystem notification, root dentry release, superblock deactivation, identifier erasure and RCU deferred mount storage release; pin killing repeatedly observes the pin list head under read protection and invokes per-pin kill until the list is empty.

Per-pin kill moves from uncompleted to kill-requested with callback invocation outside locks, treats already-completed pins as success, and otherwise queues the caller as an uninterruptible waiter that sleeps and rechecks queue membership and completion under alternating lock and read protection until woken or completion is observed.

Long term kernel mount creation builds a mount from a filesystem type name with kernel-mount semantics and then tags the resulting real mount as internally owned so its lifetime is tied to explicit unmount before filesystem unregistration rather than namespace expiry.

Early asynchronous I/O bootstrap creates a dedicated inode cache with reclaim accounting and panic-on-failure behavior, mounts an internal pseudo filesystem and aborts boot when that mount fails, then creates request and context caches and initializes related controls.

Public teardown and reclaim entries allow releasing superblock activity, draining caller supplied dentry shrink lists, transferring a dentry reference into such a list, creating timestamped anonymous inodes, obtaining fresh inode numbers, and refreshing inode change time with multigrain awareness.

Teardown validates against misuse by warning on negative aggregated mount counts, warning when children remain attached to an unmounted mount, warning when write holders remain during mount cleanup, and warning when superblock least-recently-used nodes or mount linkage linger at final passive release.

Time handling warns on invalid granularity configuration and on wake requests carrying unrecognized or multiple flag bits, clamps out-of-range seconds rather than overflowing, and the pin waiter path sleeps in uninterruptible state while ensuring the pin cannot be freed before waiter removal is observed.

Mount lifecycle uses a doomed marker for unique teardown, an internal marker selecting synchronous destruction, a kernel-mount flag for internal mounts, and an internal namespace tag marking long term mounts exempt from normal namespace expiry.

Dentry cache lifecycle uses distinct markers for shrink-list membership, least-recently-used membership, mount coverage of the dentry, and a killed state that causes direct freeing when encountered during shrink draining.

Superblock and mount context creation uses no-user, no-execution and no-device restriction flags for pseudo filesystems, a dead flag for final superblock state with a restricted wake-flag mask, and the async bootstrap uses a dedicated ring magic value as pseudo filesystem identity.

Anonymous inode identity uses user read and write permission bits with private and anonymous markers plus an initial dirty state, multigrain time uses an operation flag and a queried marker embedded in subseconds, and deferred mount release distinguishes kernel threads from normal tasks with a resume marker for task work.

Numeric and purpose constants observed include per-processor inode number batch size, nanoseconds per second for granularity comparison, filesystem context purposes for mount versus submount versus reconfigure, and a unit delay used when scheduling the delayed mount release worker.
